lesson.title: Stuck in the Old Groove: Mental Set and the Trap of a Familiar Strategy
lesson.summary: A mental set is the tendency to keep using a problem-solving strategy that has worked in the past, even when a different, more efficient approach would work better on a new problem, showing how a habit of thought can become a hindrance rather than a shortcut.
lesson.body:
A mental set is a tendency to approach a new problem using a strategy, procedure, or perspective that has successfully solved similar problems in the past, even when that approach is no longer the most efficient, or even a workable, way to solve the current problem. Where heuristics like representativeness and availability are shortcuts for judging probability, a mental set is a shortcut for choosing a method of attack: rather than evaluating a new problem completely fresh, the mind defaults to whatever strategy has been reinforced by recent or repeated success, since that strategy has a track record of working and requires no new mental effort to devise.

A classic illustrative example involves a series of problems that can all be solved using the same multi-step method. After solving several problems in a row with that method, people are given a new problem that technically can still be solved the old way, but that also has a much simpler, more direct solution available. Many solvers keep using the familiar multi-step method anyway, sometimes never even noticing the shorter path, simply because the earlier problems trained a mental set that made the longer method feel like the natural, default approach. The simpler solution is not hidden or hard to understand; it is simply overlooked, because attention and strategy selection have both been captured by the previously successful pattern.

Mental set shows up constantly outside of laboratory puzzles. A cook who has always used a particular multi-step method to soften butter may keep doing so out of habit even after learning a faster technique, simply because the old method has become the default response whenever the goal of softening butter arises. Students taught one particular procedure for solving a type of math problem often keep applying that same procedure even on problems where a much shorter approach is available and arguably more obvious, because the practiced method has become the first strategy retrieved from memory whenever a similar looking problem appears, regardless of whether it is the best option for this specific case.

Mental set persists for the same underlying reason that other cognitive shortcuts persist: retrieving and reapplying a known, previously successful strategy is fast and requires little mental effort, while searching for a genuinely new approach is slower and cognitively demanding, with no guarantee the search will actually pay off. Most of the time this trade-off favors experience, since problems that resemble past problems usually do respond well to past solutions, which is exactly why mental set develops in the first place. The cost only becomes visible in precisely the situations used to demonstrate it: a new problem that looks similar to earlier ones on the surface but that actually calls for a different, often simpler, approach that the entrenched strategy overshadows.

Mental set is a useful reminder that mental shortcuts are not limited to judgments about probability or category membership; they also shape which strategies come to mind for solving a problem in the first place, sometimes at the cost of a better available option. Representativeness, availability, and mental set are all specific examples of a much broader family of predictable patterns in how heuristics can steer thinking away from the most accurate or effective answer, a family of patterns generally referred to as cognitive biases.
